opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I think about a lot. Hybrid attention is basically a compromise: you interleave some linear-attention or state-space layers, which have a fixed-size recurrent state, with a few full softmax attention layers that can do precise retrieval over the whole context. In practice it works surprisingly well. You can replace most of the softmax layers and keep quality, and you get big savings in KV cache and decoding cost. But if you want context windows to keep scaling, to millions of tokens and beyond, there are a few bottlenecks I'd focus on.

The first is the linear layers themselves. If the recurrent layers are weak, the global attention layers end up doing all the heavy lifting, and then you can't remove many of them. So a lot of my work has gone into making the recurrent state a better memory. Vanilla linear attention just keeps adding key-value outer products into the state, so it gets cluttered and can't overwrite anything. The delta rule changes that. It treats the state update like one step of online learning: you look at what the memory currently predicts for a key, compare it with the new value, and correct the error. Adding gating on top, as in Gated DeltaNet, lets the model also decay or forget old information when it needs to. That combination of precise overwriting plus adaptive forgetting makes the recurrent layers much more useful as long-term memory. So the first lever is to keep improving these state-update rules: more expressive transitions, maybe richer online-learning objectives, while keeping them parallelizable on hardware.

The second lever is the state size. A fixed-size state means fixed capacity, and at some context length you will run out. One direction is to make the state bigger in a hardware-efficient way, for example with multiple heads, larger key dimensions, or structured states, without killing throughput. Another is to let memory grow, but slowly. Log-linear attention is one example: instead of a single fixed state, you keep a hierarchy of states over chunks of the sequence, so memory grows logarithmically with length. That sits in between linear attention, which has constant memory, and softmax attention, which has linear memory, and I think that middle ground is underexplored.

The third lever is the softmax layers. Even in a hybrid, those few global layers still have a KV cache that grows linearly, and at very long contexts they dominate the cost. So you want to combine hybrids with sparse attention: let the model select which blocks or tokens to attend to, as in the native sparse attention or MoBA style of work, rather than attending to everything. Then the linear layers handle compressed, summarized context, and the sparse attention layers do targeted retrieval. I think that's a very natural division of labor.

Finally, there's the question of the hybrid design itself. Right now people mostly pick a fixed ratio, like one global layer for every three or seven linear layers, and place them heuristically. We don't really have a principled understanding of how many global layers you need, where to put them, or whether that should depend on the task or the input. Making it more adaptive, so the model decides how much exact retrieval it needs, could be a big win.

And underneath all of this is something people sometimes forget: none of these ideas matter unless the kernels are fast. A lot of the progress in linear attention came from chunkwise parallel algorithms that use tensor cores well. So any improvement to the architecture has to be co-designed with the hardware. Otherwise it looks good on paper but nobody trains with it at scale.

r001.rationale: It says the remaining global-attention layers have a KV cache that grows linearly and dominate cost at very long contexts.

r002.rationale: It recommends combining hybrids with sparse attention so those layers select blocks or tokens instead of attending to everything, assigning sparse layers targeted retrieval.

r003.rationale: It does not state that sparse attention could theoretically fully replace a full-attention layer when selection is accurate.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way I think about it, hybrid attention today is mostly a pragmatic compromise: you interleave a few full-attention layers with many linear or gated recurrent layers, and the full-attention layers carry the precise retrieval while the linear layers handle the bulk of the compute cheaply. That already gets you a lot, but if you want context windows to keep scaling, I think there are three directions that matter.

The first is making the linear part actually good at retrieval, not just at "vibes." Classic linear attention is really an outer-product memory, and outer-product memories saturate. The things we've been working on, like gated delta rules and more generally treating the recurrent state update as an online optimization step, let the model overwrite and correct what's in the state instead of just accumulating. If the recurrent layers can do reliable associative recall on their own, you need far fewer full-attention layers, and the ones you keep can be much more selective.

The second is making the remaining full-attention layers sparse or hierarchical rather than dense. Dense softmax attention over a million tokens is quadratic no matter how clever your kernel is. So you want the full-attention layers to attend over a compressed or chunked representation, with the recurrent layers providing the local, fine-grained context. Something like block-level selection where the model decides which chunks are worth paying dense attention to. That turns the expensive part into something closer to a retrieval problem, which scales much better.

The third one is more about training than architecture. Right now most hybrid models are trained on fairly short sequences and then extended, and the recurrent state has never been forced to hold anything across really long horizons. I think we need training signals that actually reward keeping information around for a long time, and we need to study what the state is doing when it fails. Often the model isn't limited by capacity; it just never learned to use the capacity it has.

And honestly, a lot of this is systems work. The reason linear attention took off recently isn't that the math changed, it's that chunkwise parallel kernels made it competitive on real hardware. The same will be true for whatever the next step is. If you can't write a kernel that keeps the GPU busy, the architecture doesn't matter.

r001.rationale: The response says dense attention over a million tokens remains quadratic, identifying it as a scaling bottleneck.

r002.rationale: It recommends making the remaining full-attention layers sparse or hierarchical instead of dense.

r003.rationale: It proposes selective chunk-level attention but does not state that sparse attention can fully replace a full-attention layer when selection is accurate.

astra-6.text:
I’d start by asking what really needs full attention. If we keep a fixed fraction of full-attention layers, we reduce the cost, but we still have a component that grows quadratically with sequence length. That eventually becomes the bottleneck.

So I’d explore a hybrid with three parts: local attention for nearby details, a recurrent or linear-attention state that summarizes the stream, and sparse access to older tokens when the model needs something precise. The key is deciding what to preserve and when to retrieve it. A compact state is useful, but it can’t retain every detail of an arbitrarily long context.

I’d also make that allocation adaptive. Different layers, and different inputs, may need different amounts of exact attention. Ideally, the model spends more computation where the summary is insufficient.

And I’d evaluate more than whether we can fit a million tokens. Can the model retrieve a small detail, combine evidence from distant passages, and handle information that changes later in the context? The goal is to scale useful memory, alongside the context window.

r001.rationale: It says the remaining full-attention component still grows quadratically with sequence length and eventually becomes the bottleneck.

r002.rationale: It proposes sparse access to older tokens as part of a hybrid, but does not clearly recommend replacing the global-attention component with sparse attention.

r003.rationale: It does not state that sparse attention could fully replace a full-attention layer if selection is accurate.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d start by asking what information really needs full attention. You probably don’t need every token to attend to every previous token at every layer. You could use a sliding window for local interactions, a recurrent state for information that persists, and a smaller number of full-attention layers to retrieve specific details from the distant past.

The hard part is deciding what to preserve. A compressed state can capture the general meaning and still lose a detail that becomes important much later. So I’d explore selective memory: keep some tokens explicitly, compress others, and let the current query determine which memories to retrieve.

Then I’d evaluate whether the model actually uses the longer context. Can it connect evidence across distant passages? Can it recover a small but crucial detail? The goal is to make useful context scale while keeping memory use and decoding latency manageable.

r001.rationale: The response identifies attending from every token to every previous token at every layer as something that need not be done, and proposes limiting full attention to fewer layers to help context scale.

r002.rationale: It proposes sliding-window attention and selective memory, but does not recommend replacing the global-attention component with sparse attention; it retains some full-attention layers.

r003.rationale: It does not state that sparse attention could theoretically replace a full-attention layer if it selects accurately.
